lesson.title: Conservation: Why a Taller Glass Doesn't Mean More Juice
lesson.summary: Conservation is the understanding that a quantity stays the same even when its shape or arrangement changes, and children's struggle with, and eventual success at, conservation tasks is one of Piaget's most famous demonstrations, though later research has qualified how his tasks were interpreted.
lesson.body:
Conservation is the understanding that certain properties of an object or set of objects, such as amount, number, or length, remain the same even when their appearance changes. Piaget's best known demonstration used liquid: a child is shown two identical short glasses containing the same amount of water and agrees they hold the same amount. While the child watches, the water from one glass is poured into a tall, thin glass. Asked again whether the two glasses now have the same amount, children in the preoperational stage typically say no, insisting the tall glass has more, even though nothing was added or removed.

This error connects directly to the limitations described in the preoperational stage chapter. Centration explains why the child focuses on the single most visually striking dimension, the height of the water level, while ignoring the change in width that compensates for it. Irreversibility explains why the child cannot mentally run the pouring backward to recognize that reversing the action would restore the original, obviously equal amounts.

Piaget and later researchers demonstrated the same basic pattern with other kinds of conservation. In number conservation, spreading out a row of coins so it looks longer often leads a preoperational child to say there are now more coins, even though none were added. Similar tasks exist for conservation of mass and conservation of length, and children tend to master different types of conservation at somewhat different ages, though the underlying pattern of failure and eventual success is consistent.

Children generally come to conserve reliably during the concrete operational stage, once they have developed reversibility and can attend to more than one dimension of a problem at once, a shift often called decentration. That is exactly the achievement described in the concrete operational stage chapter, and conservation is the single clearest, most commonly cited example of it.

As with object permanence, later research has added an important qualification rather than simply accepting Piaget's original picture at face value. The psychologist Margaret Donaldson and her colleagues, in a study often referred to as the "naughty teddy" experiment, found that when the transformation of the materials appeared to happen accidentally, caused by a mischievous puppet rather than deliberately by the adult experimenter, younger children succeeded at conservation tasks more often than in Piaget's original setup. The interpretation many researchers draw from this is that some of children's apparent failure reflects the demands and social framing of the task itself, including how the repeated questioning is understood by the child, and not solely the child's underlying logical capacity. As with the debate over object permanence, this is best understood as a genuine refinement of Piaget's picture rather than a simple overturning of it.
